Governments use legal and diplomatic language like 'agreed locations' or 'rotational presence' to avoid calling foreign facilities military bases.

Actual Article Body:
By Mohammed Abunahel, World BEYOND War, September 18, 2026

From “Forces of allied and friendly nations” in Jordan to “agreed locations” in the Philippines and a “rotational presence” in Australia, governments use legal and diplomatic language that avoids describing facilities hosting U.S. forces as military bases. Yet changing the terminology does not change these sites’ military function.

When Jordanian Foreign Minister Ayman Safadi rejected claims that his country hosted U.S. military bases, he did not deny the presence of American troops.
